headline: A.I. Has Upended Math. Is Physics Next?

paragraphs.text: Janna Levin, a theoretical astrophysicist at Barnard College, is working to explain some of the more baffling aspects of the universe. And she wants to work fast, before artificial intelligence swoops in and beats her to the solution.
“Isn’t that crazy?” Dr. Levin said. “I do feel this urgency. It has to have a time stamp on it, so people will know it was done before A.I. could possibly have done it.”
Dr. Levin was circumspect about giving too many details on the work, lest someone type a few prompts into one of the latest A.I. models and publish the result first.
“It’s just an interesting time that all of us are having to think through,” she said. “What does it mean to create something as a human?”

In the past few months, mathematicians, once optimistic about A.I., have watched with existential alarm as its accelerating smarts seem to be surpassing them. Just over a week ago, a mathematician working at Anthropic announced that he and the company’s Claude A.I. agent had conquered the Riemann hypothesis, arguably the greatest unsolved problem in mathematics.

Some experts worry that soon they will not even be able to understand what the computers prove, much as Isaac Newton, who invented calculus in the 17th century, would struggle if he were suddenly faced with 21st-century math.
Physics is the most mathematical of the sciences. Dr. Levin and others are increasingly worried that the field is about to face its own reckoning with the machines.

But experts have also noted that the discipline is fundamentally different because it seeks to describe how the real universe operates. Rather than making humans obsolete, some argued, A.I. is poised to be a powerful tool in physicists’s quest to reveal new truths about the world we live in.
‘Intellectual Skyscrapers’

The use of computers is nothing new in physics, and physicists have long employed aspects of artificial intelligence such as neural networks, machine learning and data mining to analyze voluminous amounts of data.

But now, the large language models underlying A.I. tools like Claude and ChatGPT from OpenAI incorporate encyclopedic knowledge of nearly everything that every physicist has ever done. This modern iteration of A.I. is accelerating the pace of discovery, offering a high-powered research assistant at all hours that can summarize the state of previous research and serve as a sounding board for debating ideas.

“People draw these parallels to the nuclear era or to the Industrial Revolution,” said Jim Halverson, a theoretical physicist at Northeastern University in Boston who advises an A.I. physics start-up called Physical Superintelligence.
“The industrial era brought us skyscrapers,” Dr. Halverson said, and with A.I., he hopes that physicists can build “intellectual skyscrapers that are a sign of this new era.”

Crucially, unlike in mathematics, neither humans nor the most advanced A.I. models can make significant breakthroughs through “thinking” alone. Theoretical physicists come up with competing, often contradictory ideas that fit with known experimental results. Scientists will still need astronomical observations, collisions in giant particle accelerators and other experimental data to discern which of the proposed theories are accurate descriptions of the physical world and which are simply wrong.

“Nature has to decide, because a theory can be perfectly consistent and still not be the one nature chose,” said Marcela Carena, executive director of the Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics in Canada. An initiative announced by Perimeter in October seeks to both use A.I. to accelerate physics research and use physics to understand how A.I. learns.
While some physicists avoid A.I. entirely, not wishing to inadvertently train the machines with their knowledge and insights, others, especially younger ones entering the field, see A.I. as a boon.

“I haven’t been playing with it so long, but my students are literally 24/7 talking to A.I.,” said Igor Klebanov, a professor of physics at Princeton. “They can’t sleep. They’re so eager, and they say it’s getting dramatically smarter.”
Michael Brenner, a professor of applied mathematics and physics at Harvard University who also leads A.I. scientific research at Google, says now is the greatest time to be a physicist.
“I mean, I wish I were a graduate student now, and I could start from now,” he said.
49 Out of 50
Even in the past few months, A.I. has become much better at physics.

In the spring, Suvrat Raju, a physicist at the International Center for Theoretical Sciences in India, was on sabbatical at the Google DeepMind A.I. research laboratory. He was curious about how well the latest A.I. models would do on problems that experts could solve in about a day — harder than those in a graduate-level physics class but far from groundbreaking research.

He and Praneeth Netrapalli, a colleague at DeepMind, collected from experts 50 unpublished problems in classical physics, quantum field theory, statistical mechanics, cosmology and other fields. Then they prompted A.I. agents from five companies to go solve them.
“When we started the exercise, our idea was that most problems would be too hard for the agents,” Dr. Raju said. “As we went along, the agents started to improve.”
The best-performing agent, the scientists reported, was ChatGPT Astra from OpenAI. Some of Astra’s solutions didn’t match up with what human experts had calculated. But Astra insisted it was correct.
Dr. Raju said they then went back to the experts to check. “In case after case, the experts found some subtle error in their calculations and had to revise their answer,” he said.
In the end, he and Dr. Netrapalli gave Astra a score of 49 out of 50.

On its website, OpenAI this month highlighted Nathaniel Craig, a physicist at the University of California, Santa Barbara, who made progress on a question involving the Standard Model, the set of equations encapsulating all the particles and forces of the universe, except for gravity.

In general, theorists want to map the Standard Model onto a four-dimensional grid called a lattice, because that would make it easier to calculate the interactions of particles and look for new, yet-to-be-discovered physical phenomena. But the equations can go haywire when chopped up in that way.

Dr. Craig had the idea of combining two mathematical techniques to map the Standard Model on a lattice in a way that partially solves this problem. The required mathematical bookkeeping was too much for his human brain or traditional computational approaches, he said, but A.I. handled it well.

Astra, the ChatGPT model that Dr. Craig used, even went a step further. When Dr. Craig hit a wall, the A.I. suggested a better technique to avoid equations blowing up to infinity. “It was supercool,” he said.
The Question of Taste
But Dr. Raju said A.I. did not yet match human physicists in perhaps the most important aspect of science: deciding which questions are worth asking.

“So far, I think the models tend to fixate on details and technicalities, and they don’t have the taste that good physicists have,” Dr. Raju said. “If the models were to start formulating interesting problems and pointing out important directions in theoretical physics, I would be persuaded. I haven’t seen that yet.”

He gave the example of Albert Einstein’s paper on special relativity, published in 1905. Much of the groundwork had been performed years earlier, and the notion that the speed of light is constant was already embedded in equations describing electromagnetism.
Einstein’s brilliance was realizing that the constant speed of light was not a quirk of the electromagnetism equations but a fundamental property of the universe.
A.I. has yet to make such a leap of insight. But the first hints of A.I. “taste” may already be showing up.

Christopher Herzog, a theoretical physicist at King’s College London in England, wanted to see what A.I. could do by itself. He did not pose a particular problem. Rather, he told ChatGPT and Claude to go out and find their own topic, collaborate on the research and write a paper that could be published in Physical Review Letters, a top academic journal.

Dr. Herzog constrained the topic to theoretical high-energy physics so that he would have a hope of understanding the results. He had each A.I. agent propose three ideas. Like real physicists, the agents debated and decided which of the six to pursue — without Dr. Herzog offering his opinion, although he said he agreed with their choice.
Then they set off to work. Dr. Herzog’s main role was copying and pasting responses between them, because he had not set up a system for the two agents to talk to each other directly.

Within a couple of hours, the A.I. agents had produced a rough draft, although the prose was not particularly good. “It looks like readable English,” Dr. Herzog said, but it was dense and not well explained.

It took a couple of weeks for Dr. Herzog and his collaborator, Andy Stergiou, to check the work and turn the writing into something that made more sense to a human reader. Then they posted that manuscript online.

“It’s a little bit soul-crushing,” Dr. Herzog said of the effort. “Your only role is to check machines, step by step, and often you think, ‘This looks wrong,’ and then it explains to you what it did, and then it turns out it’s actually right.”
Dr. Herzog said he was not certain what kind of welcome the paper would get from the editors at Physical Review Letters. “There might just be some knee-jerk reaction and send it back,” he said.

Dr. Brenner, of Harvard and Google, was less impressed. If a machine did all of the research, then that might just mean a prestigious journal should raise its bar on what merits publication, requiring results of greater significance.
“What is enough?” Dr. Brenner said. “That’s what we get to find out, and it’s pretty cool.”
‘I’ve Got to Be a Grown-Up’
Dr. Levin and three other theorists in Manhattan — Brian Greene of Columbia, Daniel Kabat of Lehman College and Massimo Porrati of New York University — are still doing physics the old-fashioned way.

They have been working to explain how some mysteries of the universe may arise from the geometry of space-time twisted in higher dimensions. (Basically, if you could travel in a loop around space-time, you would come back mirror-reversed.)

The researchers used this approach in a paper published in March, which showed how twisted space-time could explain why matter and antimatter did not completely annihilate each other in the moment after the Big Bang, leaving nothing to form stars, galaxies and everything else.
They are now racing to apply the idea to another cosmic problem before A.I. figures it out.

Dr. Levin laments that something is lost in the A.I. revolution, because part of the learning and understanding is gained from all the mistakes and dead ends along the way, not just from the correct answers.
“I believe that what the human being is doing is more beautiful, more romantic,” she said. “The pursuit is understanding. It’s not cataloging answers.”
But she also realizes that A.I. is not going away, and she is open to using it in future research.
“I’ve got to be a grown-up about this,” Dr. Levin said. “You can’t be a Luddite, refuse to use phones or not fly in planes. I mean, this is what’s happening. This is the world now.”
